To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) measures of geodiverse variability improve the explanatory and predictive ability of species richness models, (2) the explanatory and predictive abilities of the species richness models can vary considerably between study areas and (3) the predictive ability of the species richness model is higher within the study areas than between the study areas.
the explanatory and predictive ability of species richness models in boreal landscapes can be enhanced by the addition of measures of geology, geomorphology and hydrology.
the inclusion of explicit measures of biodiversity in species richness models improved the explanatory power and predictive ability of these models in two study areas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of biodiversity models that are based on geodiversity measures, which can be used to predict biodiversity patterns in areas where species inventories are incomplete or non-existent.

the question of whether the explanatory and prediction power of species richness modelling can be improved by including explicit measures of geoviversity (variability in Earth surface materials, forms, and processes) in species richness models.
the question of whether geodiversity can serve as an alternative surrogate to biodiversity in modelling species richness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

geodiversity variables are useful surrogates for biodiversity in areas that are not well sampled, but that the usefulness is dependent on the type of species, the type of geodiversity, and the spatial scale of analysis.
explicit measures of geology, geomorphology and hydrology are useful predictors of biodiversity in the study areas, and that the inclusion of measures for geodiversity improved biodiversity models.

the inclusion of measures for geodiversity improves the explanatory and predictive ability of species richness models, and may provide a useful surrogate for modelling the spatial patterns of plant species richness in areas with insufficient data on biodiversity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inclusion of geodiversity variables improved the explanatory and predictive abilities of plant species richness models, but the explanatory power of the models was still limited.
the explicit measures of the geodiviersity are promising surrogates for biodiversity patterns, but their reliability is still inadequately understood.
the explicit inclusion of geodiversity in the biodiversity models improves their explanatory power, predictive accuracy, and robustness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
geodiversity is important for biodiversity and should be taken into account when planning and managing protected areas.

the inclusion of measures that reflect the variability of earth surface materials and forms, in addition to climate, topography, land cover, and other commonly used explanatory variables, improves the explanatory and predictive abilities of biodiversity models.
the inclusion of geodiversity variables in species richness models improves their explanatory power and predictive ability.
